title: Design and implement a prefix tree (Trie) supporting three operations: insert a word, search whether an exact word exists, and check whether any stored word starts with a given prefix.
keyPoints: A Trie stores words character by character along tree edges, with an end-of-word flag on each node.
Insert walks the word from the root, creating child nodes as needed, and marks the final node as a word end.
Search walks the same path and returns true only if the path exists and the final node has the end-of-word flag set.
startsWith is identical to search but returns true as long as the path exists, ignoring the end-of-word flag.
All three operations run in O(L) time where L is the key length, independent of the number of stored words.
The design choice between a HashMap of children and a fixed array of 26 trades flexibility for cache performance.

s1_definition.oneliner: A Trie stores words character by character along tree edges, with an end-of-word flag per node, giving insert, search, and prefix checks in time equal to the key length.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Trie** – a tree where each edge represents one character, so every path from the root spells a prefix.
- **End-of-word flag** – a boolean on each node marking that the prefix spelled so far is a complete stored word.
- **Insert** – walk from root, create child nodes as needed with `computeIfAbsent`, mark the final node.
- **Search** – walk the path; return true only if the path exists and the final node's flag is set.
- **startsWith** – walk the path; return true if the path exists (flag ignored).
- **Complexity** – O(L) time per operation where L is the key length, independent of stored word count.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the directory of IFSC branch codes is like a nested set of pigeonholes. Each digit typed at the counter picks the next drawer. A flag inside a drawer says whether a complete valid code ends there. Searching a code or checking whether any code begins with a few typed digits just means following the drawers.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Trie after inserting: "ICIC", "ICICI", "HDFC"

         (root)
         /    \
        I      H
        |      |
        C      D
        |      |
        I      F
        |      |
        C*     C*
        |
        I*

  * = end-of-word flag set

search("ICIC"):    I → C → I → C (isWord=true) → true
search("ICI"):     I → C → I (isWord=false) → false
startsWith("ICI"): I → C → I (exists) → true
search("ICICI"):   I → C → I → C → I (isWord=true) → true
search("ABC"):     no 'A' child at root → false
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Trie is a prefix tree where each edge carries one character, so every path from the root spells a prefix. A boolean end-of-word flag tells me whether the prefix spelled up to that node is a complete stored word. The power of this structure is that insert, search, and startsWith all cost time proportional only to the key length, never to the number of stored words.

Insert walks from the root creating child nodes as needed and marks the last node. Search walks the same path and checks the end-of-word flag. startsWith is identical but ignores the flag. The subtle distinction between search (requires flag) and startsWith (ignores flag) is what interviewers listen for.

The design trade-off between a HashMap of children and a fixed array of 26 affects flexibility and performance. HashMap handles any alphabet; the fixed array is faster and cache-friendlier for lowercase-only inputs. A senior engineer also knows about compressed Tries and concurrent variants.

At the National Bank of India, I used a Trie for type-ahead on IFSC branch codes. Each keystroke called startsWith to decide whether to keep offering suggestions and search to check for a complete valid code. The directory held hundreds of thousands of codes, so per-keystroke cost had to be independent of the directory size.

Remember one sentence: a Trie walks one character per edge, search checks the end-of-word flag, and startsWith ignores it.
